reasons: Passages verified: Vsp unit has rýðr (rjóða) ... rauðum dreyra with 'seats of the gods' as object; Il. 10.484 = 21.21 (repeated line) ἐρυθαίνετο αἵματι with earth/water as subject; OHleg skaldic quotes roðenn bloðe / rioðazc bloðe. Kroonen *reudan- 1 'make red' = Gk ἐρεύθω (*h1reudh-), OE reodan 'stain with blood', so root equation sound and Germanic shows the blood specialization. But only the verb is cognate; the blood noun is renewed (dreyri/blóð vs αἷμα), and 'X is reddened with blood' in slaughter scenes is the natural description in any language (cf. Lat. sanguine rubescere). Note the slab locus key 'fol. 2r:19 (w1/2)' is duplicated in the index (also matches the Vsp 57 sun-darkening unit); the rjóða unit is the intended one.

locus_verification.source: search-index corpora.sqlite (menota); key duplicated; rjóða unit read

known: Not known to me as a discussed formula; Homeric ἐρυθαίνετο δ' αἵματι is a repeated line.

reasons: ON passage verified: Olaf rides a white horse, it falls, fœtrner aller brotna, the king binds the horse's feet (binndr um fœtr heste sinum). Merseburg II v2 Balderes uolon sîn uuoz birenkit and AVŚ 4.12 (s4-s5 sam ... majjā majjñā ... paruṣā paruḥ; locus key is 'AVŚ, 4, 12.s5', given as 'AVŚ 4.12.s5') verified. Merseburg~AV 4.12 is a well-established parallel, but that is not this lead's anchor. The ON shares only fótr~fuoz in 'horse's foot injured while lord rides' (horse word renewed); no bone-to-bone formula, no charm language; hagiographic narrative. Scandinavian horse-sprain charms are Christianised (Jesus/saint rides), so the Olaf legend could reflect the Christian charm tradition rather than inherited wording.
known: Merseburg II ~ AV 4.12 is classic (Kuhn 1864; Watkins 1995 How to Kill a Dragon ch. on 'bone to bone'); Olaf horse-miracle link not known to me.

reasons: Verified: Vsp 'Munu ósánir akrar vaxa'; Od. 9.108-109 (no planting/ploughing, ἄσπαρτα καὶ ἀνήροτα πάντα φύονται); AVŚ 5.29.13 akṛṣṭapacye (a food-term in a list, not a narrative of spontaneous growth). Only the privative *n̥- is shared; 'sown' and 'grow' are lexically renewed, so no content-word cognate. Motif (spontaneous crops in an ideal/renewed world) is real but widely available: Hesiod Op. 117-118 automatic harvest, Lat. tellus inarata (Ovid Met. 1.109), Vergil Ecl. 4; Vsp's renewal stanza may draw on Christian/Latin golden-age imagery.
known: Golden-age 'unsown fields' comparison is commonplace in Vsp commentary; not a lexical formula.

reasons: Verified: OHleg 0057:28 'hvar er Sigurðr va ormenn' (Þormóðr on a tapestry); Grípisspá 15 'með bana Fáfnis' (index locus spelled 'Gríptsspá 15', one unit per half-line); Oddrúnargrátr 16 'þás bani Fáfnis' (indexed 'Oddrunargratr 16'); RV 1.32.1c, 2a áhan áhim. The slab sentence itself is wholly renewed (vega, ormr). The Edda leg rests on bani < *gʷʰon-: Kroonen (s.v. *banjō-) derives *banan- from *bʰon-on- and says *gʷʰ > *b is unlikely in Germanic (vs Seebold 1967). Etymology contested; serpent noun renewed (proper name). Defensible as a reflex of the HERO SLAY SERPENT formula but not compelling on the lexical side.
known: Yes: Watkins 1995 How to Kill a Dragon (*gʷʰen- *h1ógʷʰim; Germanic Sigurd/Fáfnir material discussed).

reasons: Verified Vsp 45 'Bræðr munu berjaz ... munu systrungar sifjum spilla' and Hesiod Op. 184 οὐδὲ κασίγνητος φίλος ἔσσεται. No cognate content word (bróðir vs κασίγνητος; the Greek is future of 'be' + 'dear', the Norse 'fight'). Kin-strife as a sign of the last age is generic apocalyptic topos with direct Christian source available (Mark 13:12, Matt 10:21) and Near Eastern parallels; motif-level only.
known: Vsp 45 vs Hesiod's iron age and vs Mark 13:12 is a standard comparison in Vsp commentary.

reasons: Verified: Sigvatr stanza in AM-36-fol 'bloð com varmt i víðan ... ægi'; Il. 11.266 αἷμ' ἔτι θερμὸν ἀνήνοθεν ἐξ ὠτειλῆς. Kroonen *warma- < *gʷʰor-mo- (EUR; = Lat. formus; cf. θερμός *gʷʰer-mo-), so the adjective equation is acceptable though the Germanic w- is not regular and has been doubted. Single shared element; 'warm blood' of fresh wounds is a natural description (Lat. calidus sanguis etc.). Different predicates (comes into the sea vs wells from wound). Generic.

Verified: Vsp 3 'jörð fannz æva ne upphiminn' (var-a sandr né sær); Wessobrunn 'dat ero ni uuas noh ufhimil ... noh sunna ni scein noh mano ni-liuhta'; RV 10.129.1b ná āsīt rájaḥ ná u vyòma, 2b ná rā́tryāḥ áhnaḥ āsīt praketáḥ. Germanic leg: ero~jörð (same base) + exact compound ufhimil~upphiminn in the same negated cosmogonic frame, alliterating; strong common-Germanic poetic formula (also OE upheofon). Wessobrunn is a Christian prayer (Gen 1-2 frame), so derivative risk is not nil, but the shared alliterative pair is not biblical wording. Vedic leg is only a structural parallel with renewed lexemes; negative cosmogony is also Near Eastern (Enuma Elish 1-2, Gen 2:5), so the PIE-level extension is areal-risk and should not be counted. Acceptance applies to the Germanic pair. (Lead cites a Vsp 5 sun/moon clause not in the slab unit; not checked here.)
known: Yes, well known: Wessobrunn ~ Vsp 3 is a textbook comparison; RV 10.129 and Enuma Elish parallels also discussed.

reasons: Verified: OHleg 'æyddi þau hærað ... bæðe at mannum oc at fe'; AVP 1.78.10 devāḥ manuṣyāḥ paśavaḥ ca sarve (three-part list); MBh 12.15.73 adyuḥ paśūn manuṣyān ca (beasts would eat). Etymology fine (fé = paśu- *peḱu-; maðr ~ manu-/manuṣya- *mon-/manu-). But syntax and context differ (ON 'devastate as to men and property', fé likely 'livestock/goods'; Skt list and object pair), the pairing 'people and livestock' is a near-universal inventory, and the inherited merism has *wiHro- not *man- (Av. pasu vīra, Umbr. veiro pequo), so this would be parallel renewal.
known: The 'men and cattle' merism (*wiHro- peḱu) is known (Watkins 1979; Watkins 1995); this man-/peḱu- variant not known to me.

reasons: Verified: OHleg 'hon sætr Olaf son sinn i kne seer Oc spurði'; Il. 9.488 ἐπ' ἐμοῖσιν ἐγὼ γούνεσσι καθίσσας (Phoenix feeding the infant Achilles). Both elements cognate (kné~γόνυ *ǵonu-; setja causative *sod-éye- and καθίζω *si-sd- from *sed-), same relation (adult seats child on own knee). But the gesture is universal, contexts differ (mother questioning a boy vs fosterer feeding an infant), and neither has the acknowledgment rite.
known: Child-on-knees/knee-adoption is discussed (e.g. Onians 1951 on knees; ON knésetja in legal-antiquities literature).

reasons: Verified: OHleg 'liggr þu oc sœfr' (reproach: you lie and sleep while kinsman is in fetters); Irish G303010 'Do luigh Fionn ⁊ do thuit a thoirrchiom súain ... fair' (EModIr narrative: lay down, sleep fell on him); Quintus 13.27 λεχέεσι πανύστατον ὕπνον ἴαυον (late). Etymologies fine (luigh < laigid *legh-; súan < *supno-, Matasović; ON sofa *swep-). But 'lie and sleep' is a generic pair, syntax and context differ (reproach vs narrative vs death-sleep), Irish is late prose, Greek is 3rd c. AD.

Verified Vsp 'ósánir akrar vaxa' and Od. 9.109-111 (φύονται; καί σφιν Διὸς ὄμβρος ἀέξει). vaxa ~ ἀέξω (*h2weg-s-) is a sound equation, but in Homer ἀέξει is transitive with Zeus' rain as subject in the next clause, not the crops growing unsown; the 'unsown' words are renewed. One cognate element in non-congruent syntax; golden-age motif widespread (Hesiod Op. 117-118; Lat. inarata) and Vsp renewal stanza open to Christian/Latin influence.
known: Same golden-age comparison as L003; commonplace.

reasons: Verified: OHleg 0091:10 'leðe guð hanum lios' and AM-619-4to 56r:2 'léðe guð honum lios' are the same miracle text (two Olaf-legend witnesses, near-verbatim), so not independent; Heliand 3576 'farliuui theses liohtes' (Christ heals the blind, Gospel source). ljá~farlīhan (*leykʷ-) and ljós~lioht (*lewk-) cognate, but both are Christian blind-healing contexts with a biblical model, l-alliteration explains the pairing, and the Latin lumina linquere comparison runs in the opposite sense. Derivative/learned.

Verified Vsp 3 (var-a sandr né sær ... jörð fannz æva ne upphiminn) and RV 10.129.1a-b (ná ásat āsīt ná u sát āsīt; ná āsīt rájaḥ ná u vyòma). Only the negative particle is shared; 'be' is renewed (*wes- vs *h1es-), cosmic nouns differ. Negative cosmogony is a recognized figure but also Near Eastern (Enuma Elish, Gen 2:5) and Christian (Wessobrunn), hence areal/derivative risk; figure-level only.
known: Vsp 3 ~ RV 10.129 negative cosmogony comparison is discussed in the literature.

reasons: Verified: OHleg 0027:2 'Tækr svæínenn i kne ser Oc spyr' (Olaf sets 7-year-old Halfdan on his knee and questions him); Il. 9.455 (curse: no son to sit on Amyntor's knees) and Od. 19.401 (Eurykleia puts newborn Odysseus on Autolycus' knees, who then names him). kné~γόνυ exact; verbs renewed (taka vs ἐφέζομαι/τίθημι). The ON anchor is a questioning scene, not acknowledgment; the knee-rite is also Near Eastern (Gen 30:3, 48:12, 50:23; Hurrian Ullikummi child on father's knees and named), so areal; gesture universal.
known: Knee-setting/adoption rite and Od. 19.401 widely discussed (Onians 1951; Hittite/Hurrian and biblical parallels).

reasons: Verified: OHleg 3r:12 (Ásta seats Olaf on her own knee and questions him: weak witness); AM-35-fol 115 'gaf nafn sitt hann knesetti þan svein oc fostraðe' (naming + knésetja + fostering); AM-35-fol 143 'toc Haucr sveinin Hacon oc setr a kne Aþalsteins kononge' (the Æthelstan fosterage trick); Od. 19.401-402 knees then naming. Best case of the knee set: kné~γόνυ exact in a congruent rite context (child placed on a senior male's knees, naming/acknowledgment). Verb renewed (setja vs τίθημι). Weakened by the Near Eastern distribution of the same rite (Gen 48:12, 50:23; Hurrian Kumarbi/Ullikummi), making it areal rather than diagnostic of inheritance; not a fixed wording.
known: Yes, the knee-adoption/naming rite (ON knésetja, Od. 19.401, Hurrian Ullikummi, Genesis) is discussed in the literature.

reasons: Verified: OHleg 0033:28 'bere sa sigr af aðrum i dag er sa guð vill' (Olaf's challenge to Guðbrandr); AVŚ 4.31.16 (= RV 10.84.6 Manyu hymn) sahaḥ bibharṣi. Both words cognate: Kroonen *segiz- = Skt sáhas- (*seǵh-es-), bera = bhṛ. But senses differ (ON 'carry off victory from the other' = win, an idiom bera sigr af common in ON prose incl. homilies, cf. Lat. victoriam reportare; Vedic 'you bear overpowering might' as an attribute). Index search shows sáho bibharṣi only in this one hymn (RV/AVŚ/AVP versions), not a Vedic formula; bear + abstract noun is productive. Defensible base, not compelling.

Verified: OHleg 0030:4 'ramnar munu slita ræ þitt oc vargar'; Egils saga 85r:23 'at eigi slíti dýr eða fuglar hrǽ þeirra'; Od. 24.292 θηρσὶ καὶ οἰωνοῖσιν ἕλωρ; Il. 1.4-5 κύνεσσιν οἰωνοῖσί τε. No cognate words (hrafn/vargr/hræ/slíta vs θήρ/οἰωνός/ἕλωρ). Corpse-exposure to birds and beasts is a widespread curse/threat also in Near Eastern and biblical texts (1 Sam 17:44-46, treaty curses); thematic only.
known: Beasts-of-battle theme well known (Germanic: Magoun 1955, Griffith 1993; IE comparisons in the phraseology literature).
